i took a step back to see how we can build a generalized native engine cache:

## The principled model

The research answer is one derivation contract, not one cache. Every stored derived value, point-shaped or graph-shaped, is a derived relation with four things: a dependency-complete key, a recorded input set, an output digest, and one validity rule. Point and graph queries then share the cache by sharing the relations they are computed from, never by caching answers. A point query is a keyed lookup on a materialized relation. A graph query is a demand-driven closure over the same relation. That is the Datalog view of the problem, and it matches the owner rule that data lives in SQLite rows.

Within that contract there are only three kinds of derived data, and each has a known rebuild strategy:

• Unit-local facts, keyed by content identity plus producer epoch, with no dependency set. This is Stack Graphs' per-file partial paths and Bazel-style content addressing. Bifrost already does this with per-blob resolution bundles.

• Fixpoint summaries at the unit of recursion, one per crate, SCC, or procedure. The key is the unit's own inputs; the recorded dependencies are the child units' output digests; equal output cuts off dependents. This is Salsa's early cutoff and the red-green algorithm in rustc. Bifrost's crate topology does this partially and the class-set summaries do it fully.

• Demand-shaped answers such as definition at a site, usages of a symbol, or the workspace usage graph. These are never persisted. They are recomputed per request by demand-driven composition over the two layers above, with request-lifetime memos only. Reps' magic-sets work and demand-driven pointer analysis are the basis; the owner decision on #3749 to keep usage_graph per request is the same conclusion.

The research also says what to avoid. Incrementally maintaining a recursive relation under deletion is the hard case: DRed, DBSP, IncA, and Reviser all pay for it with rederivation or counting machinery. Salsa and rust-analyzer deliberately recompute the recursive unit and rely on early cutoff instead. Bifrost should do the same. The closest paper to your exact question is Zwaan and Poulsen, OOPSLA 2023, which caches per-unit name-resolution results together with the queries each unit made against other units and reconfirms those queries on change. In Build Systems à la Carte terms that is a verifying trace, and it is exactly what the class-set summary tables already record. Glean's ownership sets are the database-resident form of the same idea.

## What the Rust engine has today

The durable layer is close to the model. Confirmed by schema and code:

• Per-blob bundles are keyed by blob OID, generation, and producer epoch, sealed in one transaction through resolution_fragment_interiors at crates/bifrost-analysis/src/analyzer/store/resolution.rs:1241-1350.

• Crate topology is keyed by a digest that folds member OIDs and consumed dependency export-surface digests at crates/bifrost-analysis/src/analyzer/store/rust_crates.rs:910-943, bound to revision intervals.

• There is no durable point-answer or graph-answer row. Both the point path and the native graph path open one selected operation and recompute from rows. That is correct under the model.

The ad hoc part is the in-process layer and the fact that two engines coexist. Confirmed:

• The legacy composition layer is still live for Rust. RustUsageWalks is constructed from crates/bifrost-analysis/src/analyzer/rust/imports.rs:83-432 and from format-macro dispatch, so import-graph-shaped queries still run through it after the flag day.

• Three uncapped, workspace-sized single-value memos survive across queries on the analyzer at crates/bifrost-analysis/src/analyzer/rust/mod.rs:178-183. That is the forbidden heap shape from the guidance, in graph paths rather than point paths.

• The same fact is memoized under two key disciplines. Usage facts are cached by generation plus OID in rust/mod.rs:192-197 and by path in store/resolution_operation.rs:818-839, and both duplicate
[... 394 bytes omitted from the middle of this message ...]
──  ────────────────────────────────
 RustAnalyzer moka caches      7        13/16
 RustWalkCaches moka caches    13       13/16
 Process statics               6        separate 32 MiB and entry caps
 Uncapped workspace memos      3        none

The durable subsystems also use four different dependency-recording disciplines: blob bundles record none, crate topology records a folded digest plus direct dependency rows, the workspace import graph is a mutable per-workspace head whose reader checks only content identity at store/import_graph.rs:1761-1765, and class-set summaries record a full child-output and read ledger. That spread is the design inconsistency, not the existence of layers. The import-graph asymmetry is a conditional risk only, since no production caller of its read method was found.

## Recommendation

1. Write the derivation contract into the architecture guidance and classify every existing derived relation as unit-local, fixpoint summary, or demand-shaped. Anything that fits none of the three is a schema gap, not a cache to add.

2. Make the crate topology a full fixpoint summary. It already folds dependency export digests; record them as rows so a dependent crate can verify its inputs without recomputing its own digest.

3. Collapse the Rust in-process caches to read-through caches keyed exactly like the row each one fronts, under one weighted budget. Delete the path-keyed duplicate of usage facts.

4. Retire the legacy walk layer for Rust or move its three uncapped memos to rows. Reverse imports belong in an eager per-blob inverted relation like resolution_rust_reverse_gap_candidates, which is the right shape for reverse demand without a cache.

5. Do not add a durable answer cache for points or graphs, and do not attempt incremental maintenance of the usage graph here. If bifrost-service caches whole graphs, it should use a complete-value key of workspace content identity plus resolver identity, replaced whole, never patched.
